articles.title: Fiery Georgia Senate debate gets personal: 4 takeaways
articles.summary: The first debate for Georgia Senate on Thursday evening quickly devolved into a string of personal attacks and campaign talking points as Sen. Jon Ossoff (D) and Rep. Mike Collins (R) wrestle for voters’ support in the closely-watched midterm race. The incumbent Democrat has maintained a lead over his GOP challenger in recent polling, but…
articles.body:
The first debate for Georgia Senate on Thursday evening quickly devolved into a string of personal attacks and campaign talking points as Sen. Jon Ossoff (D) and Rep. Mike Collins (R) wrestle for voters’ support in the closely-watched midterm race.

The incumbent Democrat has maintained a lead over his GOP challenger in recent polling, but Republicans are still holding out hope to flip this seat in November.

The candidates faced questions during the Atlanta News First debate in Atlanta about their stance on a range of issues, including artificial intelligence, border security, rural health care and agriculture.

Repeatedly, Collins and Ossoff used their allotted time to criticize each other’s family backgrounds and argue that their opponent was not fit to represent Georgia on Capitol Hill.

Here are four takeaways from their first face off:

The Democratic incumbent referred to Collins several times on Thursday evening as “the bigot congressman,” an insult he has repeatedly invoked on the campaign trail.

Ossoff pointed to the lawmaker’s past controversial social media posts, including a sharing a video from the University of Mississippi in 2024 in which a Black woman is surrounded by white students who are mimicking ape-like motions and making monkey sounds.

Collins captioned the post, “Ole Miss taking care of business.”

“If John Lewis were marching today from Selma to Montgomery, Mike Collins would be grabbing a billy club,” Ossoff said in reference to the post.

The senator also accused the Republican of promoting “Neo-Nazi propaganda,” pointing to social media posts made by his son-in-law and a former staffer.

“It’s not just that you hired half the Third Reich to staff your congressional office and you have promoted Neo-Nazi content online. It’s that you’re robbing your constituents to subsidize your donors,” Ossoff said during his response to a question about data centers.

Collins responded to a moderator question about his son-in-law’s posts, saying he “condemned racism, anti-Semitism, hate.”

“I don’t care where the source is, and I tell him that too. It’s wrong,” he said.

Collins attacks Democrat as ‘trust fund kid’

The Republican nominee called his opponent a “trust fund kid,” arguing he’s unable to understand the affordability issues faced by people in the state.

Collins reupped this criticism in response to a debate question about financial troubles facing rural hospitals in the state.

“You know the problem is, and Jon Ossoff won’t understand this because he doesn’t have to worry about health care,” he said. “He doesn’t have to worry about trying to buy health care insurance for his family. He never will.”

Ossoff hit back, claiming his opponent “inherited a seat in Congress” during his closing statement. The Republican’s father is Mac Collins, the late Georgia lawmaker who served 12 years in the House.

Collins and Ossoff hit one another over their legislative record on affordability, as rising costs of living across the country remain top of mind for voters ahead of Election Day.

The Democrat pointed to rising diesel and fertilizer costs amid the Iran war and the Trump administration’s tariffs.

“As we speak right now, it’s Georgia farmers bearing the brunt of the Mike Collins-Donald Trump tariffs,” Ossoff said. “Just like it’s Georgia farmers bearing the brunt of these high diesel prices.

The Republican nominee placed blame on last year’s government shutdown, which he and other congressional lawmakers have accused Democrats of causing.

“He shut it down, y’all,” Collins said. “Right when we were trying to get that emergency money out for Hurricane Helene so that our farmers and our small communities could repair and prepare for this year’s harvest.”

Collins skirts question about 2020 election

Ossoff put his opponent on the spot during Thursday’s debate about his support for President Trump’s unsubstantiated claims of voter fraud in the 2020 presidential election, including in Georgia’s Fulton County.

“Mike Collins is one of the most extreme members of Congress,” the Democrat said. “He’s a Trump puppet election denier. I want to hear if Mike still believes the 2020 election was stolen. What do you say, Mike?”

Ossoff turned to face his opponent, who stared down at his notes before a moderator asked him a new question about The Laken Riley Act he introduced.

articles.body:
President Trump said Thursday that Minnesotans should “fight back” against Somali immigrants following previous attacks against the group.

“The once Great State of Minnesota is being taken over by Somali Immigrants. There is Violence, Murder, and Mayhem all over the State,” Trump wrote on Truth Social . “The people of Minnesota must fight back.”

He added that Minnesota’s residents were “abandoned” by the state government, and Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz (D) was “an incompetent thief who doesn’t want to get involved.”

“[Walz] just wants to get out of town with as much as he can steal, and then, lead a quiet life,” Trump continued. “The Somalians should not be allowed to get away with what they are doing. They view you as weak and stupid people. Fight back Minnesota, fight back! If you need, the Federal Government will come to your rescue.”

“Governor Tim Walz, and Mayor of Minneapolis, Jacob Frey, must immediately ask for Federal help — and leave the rest to us,” he concluded.

The Somali community has been targeted by the Trump administration due to a massive pandemic-era fraud scheme that stole hundreds of millions from a federally funded nutrition program. As much as $1 billion is reported to have been stolen in separate plots.

Trump previously slammed the Somali community in 2025, referring to Minnesota Rep. Ilhan Omar (D) as “ garbage ,” and that Somalia “stinks.”

The Trump administration ended temporary protected status (TPS) for Somali holders in January. Former Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Kristi Noem said at the time that continuing TPS protections were “contrary to our national interests.”

Walz accused Trump in 2025 of “ demonizing ” Somali migrants in Minnesota.

“As far as demonizing our Somali community, maybe, he could help us on some things,” Walz said at the time. “Demonizing an entire community, folks who are in the professions, educators, artists, doctors, lawyers, entrepreneurs, they bring the diversity and the energy to a place like Minnesota.”

According to World Population Review , Minnesota has the largest population of Somalis at 1.07 percent concentrated primarily in the Minneapolis-St. Paul area. Most of the population arrived in the U.S. as refugees after a civil war in Somalia throughout the 1990s.

articles.title: Michigan Senate debate goes off the rails: 4 takeaways
articles.summary: Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed’s first Senate debate in Michigan turned so contentious it even extended off camera. “In 30 years of doing debates, I’ve never seen it continue during the commercial,” WOOD TV moderator Rick Albin said. “But it did” Rogers and El-Sayed participated in a debate hosted by Nexstar’s Grand Rapids…
articles.body:
Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed’s first Senate debate in Michigan turned so contentious it even extended off camera.

“In 30 years of doing debates, I’ve never seen it continue during the commercial,” WOOD TV moderator Rick Albin said. “But it did”

Rogers and El-Sayed participated in a debate hosted by Nexstar’s Grand Rapids station where the pair lobbed personal attacks centering on corporate and foreign influence, carpetbagging, President Trump and their professional careers.

El-Sayed looked to make the debate a referendum on the president by tying Rogers to Trump while the GOP candidate sought to cast himself as bipartisan while characterizing the Democrat as dishonest. Last month, the Democrat took the debate stage alone after Rogers declined to participate , accusing the host outlet of bias.

The pair will square off one more time before the election on Oct. 21 in a debate hosted by WXYZ-TV.

Here’s four takeaways from the first Michigan Senate debate:

The debate ended where it started — feisty and spirited — as the two men immediately launched into personal attacks.

El-Sayed chided Rogers at multiple points, telling him to “be serious, my guy” while suggesting the former congressman was beholden to the president. The former Wayne County health official also brought up Rogers’ past Florida residence, suggesting he was a carpetbagger.

“I’ve been absolutely clear. I want our tax dollars spent here to provide schools here, and by here, I mean Michigan, not Florida,” El-Sayed said during the debate when asked if he would vote to provide Israel with defensive arms if attacked.

The Democrat described Rogers as a “rubber stamp” for Trump that is beholden to corporate interests.

Meanwhile, Rogers suggested that El-Sayed, who received a medical degree from Columbia University and a doctorate in public health at Oxford University, was falsely parading as a medical professional. El-Sayed has previously received scrutiny for calling himself a “physician” despite not practicing medicine.

“And the doctor — well, he’s not really a doctor.” Rogers said during the debate.

“Matter of fact, if somebody came into his office and he tried to treat that patient, he’d go to jail. So, listen to this guy and what he’s trying to sell here today,” Rogers added later.

Rogers also baselessly alleged that El-Sayed and his family have ties to the Muslim Brotherhood. Bridge Michigan reported last month that there was no evidence that El-Sayed has direct ties to the group.

The Republican appeared at one point to almost go as far as to suggest that El-Sayed, who is Muslim, could have terrorist family relatives.

“Those programs were really, really important in catching people who were suspected of terrorists and being terrorist — committing a terrorist act, that’s really, really important,” Rogers said when asked about his position of guardrails on flock cameras.

“And why would that bother you? Well, if you have someone in your family that might be on —” Rogers added, before El-Sayed, chimed in.

“Go ahead and say it,” El-Sayed said at one point, adding, “You’ve been tiptoeing around it the whole time, just say it.”

The progressive frequently invoked the president, as Republican candidates across the country grapple with Trump’s underwater approval ratings.

“It’s about whether or not you trust your next U.S. senator [to] stand up to Trump and Trumpism,” El-Sayed said.

“But when [you’re] running because Donald Trump called you and asked you to run, you can tell he’s not going to stand up to anybody,” he added

At another point, El-Sayed called Rogers a “sock puppet for the Trump administration” while talking about the Republican and Trump’s war in Iran.

The former congressman, who is endorsed by the president, has sought to walk a tight rope with Trump amid his unpopularity. Earlier this week, Rogers called for an end to the trade war with Canada , and he previously called for the conflict in Iran to come to an end.

During the debate, Rogers said he called Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and pushed for a deal on tariffs with Canada.

“I would like to see the deal made,” he said, later adding that, “Canada still has some high tariffs for U.S. goods, and they did it before this started. Those should be eliminated. There are tariffs that I think are too high and not helpful for us. We ought to get rid of those.”

Rogers: Minnesota immigration crackdown ‘not appropriate’

Another notable point during the debate was Rogers’s break with the Trump administration over its immigration crackdown , suggesting that actions taken by the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in Minnesota had gone too far.

“I think the public efforts in Minnesota were probably not appropriate. I actually did fugitive raids when I was an FBI agent in Chicago. You always want to go in quiet, get the bad guy, get out of the neighborhood for less problems,” Rogers said. “So that’s — that to me was something that they could have done differently.”

The former congressman suggested that they later corrected their tactics.

Several shootings involving federal immigration enforcement officers, including two in Minnesota, have sparked scrutiny of the Trump administration as critics have argued that the White House’s crackdown on immigration has gone too far. On Thursday, a man was shot by ICE in New York.

El-Sayed sidesteps question on Israel, Iran

El-Sayed avoided answering a question on whether he saw Iran or Israel as the bigger threat when pressed multiple times on the debate stage, before suggesting that both countries were “dangerous” to the U.S.

“I’m just going to say that that’s a ridiculous hypothetical because here’s what’s happening right now: Our ostensible ally in Israel has lobbied us to go to war with Iran,” El-Sayed said. “We have watched as Iran has responded by bombing all kinds of countries in the Middle East and then choking off the world’s energy supply. So, this is a situation in which I don’t think we should be a part.”

Pressed again later, El-Sayed criticized the question before saying both were a threat.

“I think both of them have proven dangerous in their own way. One at risk of attacking us. One getting us into wars we have no business fighting,” he said.

articles.title: Second Maine Senate debate takes testy turn: 3 takeaways
articles.summary: Republican Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson squared off Thursday in the second Maine Senate debate of the week, sparring over the Iran war and high prices as their battleground race barrels toward Election Day. The hourlong debate, hosted by WMTW, turned testy at times as the rivals defended their records and re-upped many…
articles.body:
Republican Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson squared off Thursday in the second Maine Senate debate of the week, sparring over the Iran war and high prices as their battleground race barrels toward Election Day.

The hourlong debate, hosted by WMTW, turned testy at times as the rivals defended their records and re-upped many of their night-one talking points about abortion, immigration and the economy. Collins stressed that she’s often at odds with her party, while Jackson highlighted her alignment with President Trump.

The stakes were high for both candidates to avoid on-stage gaffes and snag strong clips that could move the needle of the close race. Decision Desk HQ’s polling averages show Jackson, who became the party’s pick after their initial nominee withdrew this summer, leading the five-term incumbent by just over a point in the blue-leaning Pine Tree State.

Here are three takeaways from the latest debate, with two more showdowns scheduled later this month:

Senate hopefuls battle over Iran war: ‘You owe me an apology’

The rivals clashed over remarks on the Iran war and its economic impacts on Mainers struggling under high prices.

As the candidates debated how to address record-high heating oil prices , moderator Jon Chrisos pressed Collins over her Senate votes on Trump’s military moves in Iran.

She stressed that she has “voted nine times to end this war” under the War Powers Act. A live fact-check from PolitiFact, though, called her claim “selective counting ,” pointing to five times Collins voted against such resolutions.

“She could use her leverage to stop this war. But instead, they’re making money,” Jackson argued during the debate. “I mean, Senator Collins and her husband [are] making money, more, off of this war, and so is a whole bunch of other people, and that’s why this doesn’t, doesn’t stop.”

“That is absolutely outrageous, and you owe me an apology,” the senator said.

“No, you owe me an apology,” Jackson replied.

Jackson did not offer specific evidence for his claim that Collins was profiting from the war.

PolitiFact noted that the senator’s husband, Thomas Daffron, owns stock in Boeing and RTX, both defense contractors for the U.S. Military, according to reporting from The Maine Independent. A spokesperson told the outlet last month that Collins has “never bought, sold or owned” any individual stock shares as senator, and that her husband’s investments “are made exclusively by a third-party advisor without his consultation.”

Jackson pointed to the war — which is deeply unpopular among midterm voters — at multiple points in the night, stressing that “we have to get out of Iran” to bring down fuel prices, and raising concerns that “people will freeze to death this winter because they can’t afford to heat their home.”

Collins, though, cast doubt on the Iran war as the main driver of high electric rates in Maine, casting blame on moves from the state Legislature, where Jackson served as Senate president.

“It’s just not accurate to say that it’s the Iran war that has caused Maine to have the fourth highest electric bills in the country. If it were the Iran War, why wouldn’t New Hampshire and other states have the same level of electric bills that Maine has?” Collins asked.

Thirty years ago, Collins pledged she would only serve for two terms if elected to the Senate. Now, she’s going for a sixth six-year term.

“What I learned is how much more effective I could be as the seventh ranked person in the Senate versus 99th, which is what I was when I first started out,” Collins said, when asked on the debate stage about what changed her mind.

Touting some of her more recent legislative achievements, including becoming the first Maine senator to chair the powerful Appropriations Committee, she said “I couldn’t have done this in the early years in the Senate.”

Collins was reelected in 2014 by nearly 40 points, but won her 2020 bid by a comparatively slim 9 points. She’s now considered one of the most vulnerable senators in the 2026 cycle.

But Jackson also faced questions about what was behind his bid. After running unsuccessfully for governor this cycle, the Democrat was named as his party’s replacement nominee after Graham Platner, a progressive oyster farmer who won the initial primary, withdrew amid sexual misconduct allegations.

“Why should voters see this as your own campaign and not something that you inherited?” Chrisos asked.

“Well, it isn’t my own campaign. I mean, it’s the people across Maine,” Jackson replied. “This is not about Troy Jackson. It’s not about Graham Platner. What it is about is Donald Trump and Susan Collins and the band that are making life so much harder in the state.”

Collins, Jackson respond to controversial reports

Both candidates responded to recent reports that have raised questions about both candidates’ financial moves in the run-up to Election Day.

Collins denied recent reporting that accused her of receiving illegal campaign contributions, calling the claims “absolutely false.”

ProPublica reported in September that, after a former CEO of defense contractor Navatak made a 2019 donation to a Collins super PAC, Collins used her position on the Appropriations Committee to award military contracts to the company.

Martin Kao pleaded guilty in 2022 to making illegal campaign contributions. The FBI at the time found nothing implicating Collins or her campaign — but Chrisos questioned what Collins would say to voters who think the report raises questions about her campaign financing.

“Well, they don’t, and these allegations are absolutely false, and they’ve been proven false. But Troy and Chuck Schumer keep running false ads to try to convince you otherwise,” Collins said.

She said that the University of Maine had come to her with a proposal for research with Navatek, and that Kao is “in jail today, where he belongs.”

Jackson, too, responded to new reporting about donations to a PAC he was involved in during his service in the Maine Legislature.

The Washington Post reported that, up until two years ago, the Democrat used a PAC that accepted funds from tobacco, pharmaceutical and other big companies and affiliated PACs — though he openly rejects corporate PAC money in the Senate race.

Asked what he’d say to voters who think his role in the PAC raises questions, Jackson said that the PAC “is a group of people.”

“I didn’t make decisions on who or what, when we were going to take money,” he said.

articles.title: Arlington County sues to block Trump arch after project gets key approval
articles.summary: Arlington County has filed a lawsuit to block President Trump’s proposed triumphal arch following the project’s approval by the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts in April. The lawsuit opposed the construction of the proposed 250-foot arch, citing concerns about the project’s impact on tourism and safety to local residents. “Using the Arch to store large…
articles.body:
Arlington County has filed a lawsuit to block President Trump’s proposed triumphal arch following the project’s approval by the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts in April.

The lawsuit opposed the construction of the proposed 250-foot arch, citing concerns about the project’s impact on tourism and safety to local residents.

“Using the Arch to store large stockpiles of ammunition and as a staging point for drones and snipers, so close to commuters and tourists, will dramatically worsen these public-safety harms and the risk of accidents,” attorneys for Arlington County wrote in a complaint .

“The Arch will…directly obstruct the line of sight between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery that was deliberately created to symbolize the nation’s post-Civil War reunification,” the lawyers continued.

The legal team stated that Arlington County’s 245,000 residents would be “harmed by increased traffic” near the project’s site at Memorial Circle.

The lawsuit named the Department of the Interior and its Secretary Doug Burgum alongside the National Park Service (NPS) and acting director Jessica Bowron as defendants.

“At a time when millions of Americans are struggling to make ends meet, we don’t need vanity projects. This project will do significant harm to the people of Arlington County,” Skye Perryman, president and CEO of Democracy Forward, an organization suing with the county, said in a press release on Thursday.

This is not the first lawsuit against the proposed arch, as a group of Vietnam War veterans sued in September for an emergency court order to block the project from breaking ground.

They also sued in February , similarly arguing that the location of the arch would block historical sightlines between the Lincoln Memorial, Arlington National Cemetery and Arlington House.

The NPS backed the arch’s proposed location earlier this fall, but also found the monument would have “ adverse effects ” on several historic sites as well as the skyline of the nation’s capital.

The arch is one of Trump’s projects as part of his efforts to “Make D.C. Safe and Beautiful Again.” Other projects included renovations at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool , an ongoing legal battle over changes to the Kennedy Center and choosing to pave over the White House Rose Garden .

articles.title: Brazilian Supreme Court judge issues arrest warrant for Eduardo Bolsonaro
articles.summary: Arrest warrant for presidential candidate’s brother is issued weeks before Brazil’s runoff election.
articles.body:
A Brazilian Supreme Court justice has issued an arrest warrant for Eduardo Bolsonaro , brother of presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro, a move likely to heat up the hard-fought race.

Justice Alexandre de Moraes issued the arrest warrant on Thursday, weeks before a runoff election for the country’s presidency between incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Flavio Bolsonaro, the favourite to win .

In June, the Brazilian Supreme Court convicted Eduardo Bolsonaro on charges of lobbying the US to interfere in the trial of his father, former right-wing President Jair Bolsonaro.

Eduardo Bolsonaro has been a key link between his brother and the Trump administration, accompanying him to a May meeting with US President Donald Trump at the White House.

Both sides of Brazil’s deeply polarised partisan divide have long accused each other of corruption and lawfare as political drama reaches a crescendo in the buildup to the October 25 runoff.

In March 2025, Eduardo Bolsonaro pledged he would move to the US full time to “focus 100 percent” of his energy on freeing his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro.

The move cost him his seat in the Brazilian National Congress and his job as a federal police investigator.

The 42-year-old former lawmaker lives in Texas and is a green card holder.

He was convicted of lobbying to impose sanctions on members of the Brazilian government and to implement higher tariffs on the country’s exports during the trial of his father.

De Moraes, whom the Bolsonaro family regards as a political enemy, chaired the investigation that led to Jair Bolsonaro being sentenced in September 2025 to 27 years in prison for plotting to stage a coup.

The justice said in his ruling that Eduardo Bolsonaro should start serving his four-year sentence immediately.

“The defendant cannot benefit from his own wrongdoing by fleeing the national territory to an unknown location for the purpose of thwarting the application of criminal law,” de Moraes said.

De Moraes also cancelled Eduardo Bolsonaro’s Brazilian passport and instructed the country’s federal police to arrest him if he returns to Brazil.

Beyond disgusting,” he wrote on social platform X. “Public executions are…
articles.body:
Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) on Thursday slammed the recent decision by the U.S. military to livestream the upcoming execution of convicted Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan, calling it “beyond disgusting.”

“Hasan should face the death penalty, but making his execution public and streaming it? Beyond disgusting,” he wrote on social platform X . “Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do. It should not be happening in America.”

Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist who opened fire at the Fort Hood base in Texas in 2009 and killed 13 people, is set to be put to death on Dec. 3, according to the U.S. Army . He was found guilty in 2013 of 45 counts of premeditated murder and attempted premeditated murder, dismissed from the Army and given a death penalty sentence.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced Thursday the execution, by firing squad, would be open to the public . It is set to take place at Fort Hood.

“We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things,” Hegseth told Real America’s Voice onboard the USS Abraham Lincoln.

Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.) criticized the Pentagon chief’s decision to livestream the event, also calling it “disgusting” later Thursday.

“What, is he mimicking ISIS executions? I mean, I understand that in this country we have the death penalty, but public execution is medieval,” Murphy said in an appearance on CNN’s “Erin Burnett OutFront.”

“That is just absolutely extraordinary, galling,” he continued, “No matter whether you support or oppose the death penalty, public hangings and executions? That’s what America has become? … That’s pretty extraordinary.”

Army rules allow for at least two media outlets to be present for an execution, but none has been broadcast live in the U.S. The nation’s last public execution was in 1936.

There are currently only four others sitting on the U.S. military’s death row, with Hasan being the most recently sentenced to death, according to the Death Penalty Information Center .

articles.title: In our current system, Congress’s crazy behavior is actually rational
articles.summary: To transform an underperforming Congress into a highly productive legislature, we must change politicians’ electoral incentives.
articles.body:
There’s no shortage of vital issues facing our country at the moment: rising gas prices, the ongoing war in Iran, concerns on the unfettered expansion of artificial intelligence. This is to say nothing of longer-term issues like immigration, healthcare and housing affordability, that continue to go untouched.

Meanwhile, Congress, the institution constitutionally assigned to tackle these vexing national problems, is nowhere to be found. Both the House and Senate are closed, and their members are off campaigning for re-election.

Unsurprisingly, the disparagement of Congress is unrelenting. Only 16 percent of Americans approve of the job Congress is doing. Critics claim that members are either uninterested in doing their job or more focused on showboating and gaining social media impressions than legislating.

But we may be looking at the problem the wrong way. Yes, legislators have chosen to campaign rather than govern. Yes, many of them devote substantial portions of their time to dishing out insults on social media, playing gotcha in hearings and attending fundraisers with deep-pocketed interests.

Icky as all those things are, they are rational behaviors designed to improve their odds of being re-elected. As we found in a recent report issued by American Enterprise Institute and the Stavros Niarchos Foundation Agora Institute at Johns Hopkins, members are strategic actors reacting to the incentives before them.

Legislators want to persuade enough voters to pick them on the ballot. This is why they are back in their home states raising money to run campaign ads rather than debating and deciding what to do about our nation’s problems.

But why are legislators not trying to get re-elected by making good policy? The answer is that making good policy is challenging, and the definition of good policy itself is not clear cut. The sheer math of persuading a majority of the House of Representatives, the Senate and the president to approve a bill is difficult enough. It becomes all the more challenging when legislators feel that voters will punish them for bargaining with members of the other party.

It is far easier for our representatives and senators to campaign than govern. This is why they are back home claiming credit for the good things happening in America, such as the rising median household income , and shifting blame to the other party for the bad things such as high interest rates .

Voters are not going to make legislators do a better job by grumbling and complaining. Nor is throwing the bums out a long-term solution. For more than three decades, voters have replaced incumbent legislators with fresh faces and shifted control of the House and Senate from Democrats to Republicans and back again.

To transform an underperforming Congress into a highly productive legislature, we must change politicians’ electoral incentives.

First, substantial evidence indicates that the structure of our congressional elections exacerbates legislative underperformance. Primary elections are a big part of the dysfunction.

Only around 20 percent of voters participate in these preliminary elections, and these voters tend to be more ideologically extreme than the average American. Frequently they also are single-issue voters who will only vote for and donate to a candidate who full-throatedly supports their position on abortion, guns or transgender rights.

Unsurprisingly, then, primary elections encourage members of Congress to stake out positions that are further to the left and right and to avoid bargaining with members of the opposite political party. They also tend to discourage more moderate candidates from running for Congress and reward those who are skilled at raising money from deep-pocketed interest groups.

Second, Americans need to take a long look in the mirror and recognize that we are part of Congress’s incentive problem. Fewer than half of us vote in midterm congressional elections. An abundance of evidence indicates that we are polarized around hot button issues, and that political extremists amongst us have fooled us into thinking we are way more divided on politics than we actually are.

A recent poll found that 63 percent of Democrats agree or strongly agree that Republicans are not just bad for the country but downright evil, and 57 percent of Republicans agree with the same sentiment about Democrats.

Although more of us register as independents than either Democrats or Republicans, we vote like reliable partisans. We voters were once happy to vote for the best candidate — ticket splitting occurred in more than 100 congressional districts in each presidential election from 1972 through 1996. But in 2024, only 16 of 435 congressional districts supported a presidential candidate of one party and a House candidate from another party.

It does not have to be this way. We should reform or replace primaries with electoral systems that better incentivize legislators to work for us. We also should get off the couch and show up to vote and quit letting ourselves be fooled into voting for people who are more interested in trash-talking the other party than trying to solve important national problems.

The U.S. is a representative democracy. Ultimately, the Congress we get is the Congress we choose.

Scott Warren is a professor of practice at the Stavros Niarchos Foundation Agora Institute at Johns Hopkins University. Kevin R. Kosar is a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute. They are the authors of the report “ Congress Is Struggling to Govern. Are Electoral Incentives to Blame?”

articles.title: Mamdani: ‘No explanation’ for ICE shooting man near child in New York
articles.summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) late Thursday condemned the recent shooting of a man in the city by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer. “There is no explanation for these tactics. There is no explanation for federal officers firing this many rounds into a car that has a 5-year-old in the car.…
articles.body:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) late Thursday condemned the recent shooting of a man in the city by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer.

“There is no explanation for these tactics. There is no explanation for federal officers firing this many rounds into a car that has a 5-year-old in the car. There is no explanation,” Mamdani said at a press conference about the shooting Thursday night.

“And the pretext of ICE is, in their words, ‘to keep this country safe.’ How is it keeping anyone safe to have — as you just heard from the police commissioner [Jessica Tisch] — individuals wearing construction vests in masks with long guns,” the mayor continued. “Residents have no idea if these are law enforcement agents, or if they are simply attacking someone on the street.”

A reporter then asked Mamdani about a recent post when he said he called President Trump and Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin about the shooting.

“Now I made clear to the president, to the secretary, our request that ICE agents leave the scene entirely, as well as the demand that ICE stop its enforcement actions in New York City,” the Democratic mayor said, adding that the phone call lasted for two hours.

He added his negotiations for the release of the man shot by the officer were “unsuccessful.”

The incident happened around 4 p.m. EDT Thursday in the Marble Hill neighborhood, where an ICE officer attempted to arrest a man Tisch identified during the press conference as 28-year-old Oscar Belgal, while he was in a car. There was a 5-year-old boy, who is believed to be his son, in the back seat of the vehicle.

The police commissioner said a preliminary investigation revealed at least one ICE officer fired seven rounds into the car and hit Belgal in the neck below his left ear. The child was not injured and is now with another family member.

The DHS said in a statement on social platform X that it was “conducting a targeted enforcement operation” to arrest a man with “prior criminal conviction for grand larceny, and multiple prior arrests for assault, robbery, possession of drugs, and weapons possession.”

“The individual is alive and at a local hospital,” the department added.

The Trump administration announced in September it would ramp up its presence in “ sanctuary cities ” — including parts of New York.

Since Trump returned to the White House, ICE officers broke records with back-to-back months of arrests topping 50,000 in July and August, according to the Deportation Data Project . In the president’s second term, federal immigration officers have also shot at least 20 people, seven of them fatally, the data shows.

articles.body:
President Trump slammed Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (D) following the first debate between him and his opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.), on Thursday evening.

“Mike Rogers, the great American Patriot and Republican Candidate for the U.S. Senate from Michigan, completely obliterated Mohammed El-Sayed in the big debate tonight,” Trump wrote on Truth Social shortly after midnight, using his preferred nickname for the Democratic nominee.

“If this was a fight they would have stopped it. Mohammed is a Jihadist lunatic who hates our Country, the Black People of Detroit, and wants to see the U.S. fail,” the president continued. “Short on Stature, Patriotism, and Truth, Mohammed’s statements have been loaded up with lies and deceit.”

Trump has repeatedly referred to the Democrat as “Mohammed” during the race. El-Sayed, whose full name is Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed, has accused the president of using his name and Muslim faith to “distract” from rising costs under the Trump administration.

“He knows my name is Abdul. He says it everyday,” the progressive candidate wrote in a social media post , after the president referred to him as “Mohammed” again ahead of the debate.

“He thinks so low of us,” he continued. “He thinks he can use my name and my faith to distract us from the suffering his policies are inflicting on us at the pump, at the grocery store, and at the doctor’s office. He thinks we don’t know any better. It’s time for change.”

During the forum, El-Sayed accused his Republican opponent of being a “rubber stamp” for the president and attempted to tie Rogers’s positions to the White House, as Trump faces a historic decline in approval ratings ahead of the midterms.

“It’s about whether or not you trust your next U.S. senator [to] stand up to Trump and Trumpism,” he said. “But when [you’re] running because Donald Trump called you and asked you to run, you can tell he’s not going to stand up to anybody.”

Rogers, in response, tried to showcase several points of disagreement with the Trump administration during the exchange, pointing to his call this week to end the trade war with Canada and suggesting that the mass federal immigration crackdown had gone too far at times.

articles.title: 78 percent blame Trump policies for rising prices: Survey
articles.summary: Nearly 8 in 10 Americans blame the Trump administration for rising costs of living across the country, according to a poll released Friday. The Reuters survey found 78 percent of respondents in the U.S. — including 64 percent of Republicans, 76 percent of independents and 95 percent of Democrats — believe some of the responsibility…
articles.body:
Nearly 8 in 10 Americans blame the Trump administration for rising costs of living across the country, according to a poll released Friday.

The Reuters survey found 78 percent of respondents in the U.S. — including 64 percent of Republicans, 76 percent of independents and 95 percent of Democrats — believe some of the responsibility for hiked prices lies with the White House.

President Trump’s economic approval rating has taken historic hits amid the ongoing Iran war, which has sent global energy rates skyrocketing, and his administration’s decision to hike tariffs on trading partners like Canada.

These plummeting approval ratings could pose problems for Republicans on the ballot this November as the GOP fights to retain control of Congress.

Several candidates in tight races have broken with the president on issues like tariffs, with Michigan Senate GOP nominee Mike Rogers calling on the administration this week to end its economic fight with Canada “now.”

In the Reuters poll, 62 percent said they disapproved of how the president has handled the economy, including about 25 percent of Republicans and 92 percent of Democrats.

Fifty-seven percent of GOP respondents said their living costs have been increasing faster than their paychecks have under the second Trump administration. Two-thirds of the poll’s general survey population said the same.

The average price of standard gas and diesel has skyrocketed in the U.S. amid the Trump administration’s ongoing military operations against Iran, which has effectively stalled the flow of oil trade through the Strait of Hormuz.

Regular gas was up to an average of $4.37 per gallon on Friday — more than a 40 percent increase from a year ago, according to AAA . Diesel was up to around an average of $6.28 per gallon on Friday.

The six-day Reuters/Ipsos poll, conducted online and nationwide and completed on Monday, gathered responses from 4,506 U.S. adults. It had a margin of error of 2 percentage points for all respondents and 3 points for Republicans, Democrats and independents.

articles.title: There’s no mail on Monday as USPS observes federal holiday
articles.summary: Regardless of whether you have a three-day weekend ahead of you or not, there is one task you can skip on Monday: checking your mailbox.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) — Regardless of whether you have a three-day weekend ahead of you or not, there is one task you can skip on Monday: checking your mailbox.

In case you haven’t looked at a calendar recently, Monday is Columbus Day. It’s not only a day when you may not have to work, but one of several holidays observed by federal offices and banks.

Among those observing the holiday will be the U.S. Postal Service, leaving you without any new political fliers or bills in your mailbox on Monday.

Other delivery services, like FedEx , UPS , and Amazon , will be available.

Banks, meanwhile, will also likely be closed for the day. Local services, like libraries, may also take the day off. It’s best to confirm hours and availability online or by calling ahead.

President Trump brought Columbus Day “back from the ashes” last spring, accusing Democrats of doing “everything possible to destroy Christopher Columbus” and “his reputation.”

In 2021, President Biden became the first president to declare the second Monday of October as Indigenous Peoples Day .

An increasing number of Americans have, in recent years, opted to observe Indigenous Peoples Day instead of Columbus Day, pointing to the violence explorer Christopher Columbus inflicted on Native communities, The Hill previously reported .

Columbus Day will happen a day earlier next year, landing on Oct. 11. The next federal holiday this year, meanwhile, is Veterans Day on Nov. 11.

articles.title: 26 percent of Trump voters say GOP candidates should break from him: Survey
articles.summary: More than one-fourth of President Trump’s 2024 voters believe Republicans would be more likely to win the midterms if they break away from the president this November, a Politico-PF Global poll found. Twenty-six percent of respondents who voted for the president in 2024 said the Republican in their district would have a better chance of…
articles.body:
More than one-fourth of President Trump’s 2024 voters believe Republicans would be more likely to win the midterms if they break away from the president this November, a Politico-PF Global poll found.

Twenty-six percent of respondents who voted for the president in 2024 said the Republican in their district would have a better chance of winning if they turned their back on Trump. On the issues, 57 percent said Republicans should break with Trump over the Iran war, 61 percent said they should break with him over the economy and 67 percent said so over immigration and border control.

Less than a month from the midterm elections, Republicans are working to defend seats — like those for Senate in Kansas and Iowa — that were not seen as competitive just a few months ago. Trump’s low approval ratings and discontent with the state of the economy are helping to give Democrats a chance to win in such places.

Despite the strong poll numbers, Democrats have not regained popularity among Americans. Democrats carry a 43.8 percent favorability rating, according to Decision Desk HQ .

The poll — which surveyed 2,001 respondents in early October — carries a 2.2 point margin of error with larger margins of error for the smaller subgroups.

Asked who should get credit if Republicans keep their majorities in the House and Senate this November, 22 percent of respondents said it would be because of Trump’s actions as president, while 29 percent said it would be because Democrats had run a weak campaign. Twenty-three percent said credit should be given to the fact that Republicans ran strong campaigns and not because of Trump, and 26 percent said they don’t know who should get credit.

The poll found that 44 percent of respondents said their financial situations have gotten worse or much worse since Trump took office last year, while 21 percent said their situations have gotten better or much better.

Fifty-nine percent of respondents said groceries, gas and other expenses have gotten somewhat or much less affordable since Trump took office, including 40 percent of Trump 2024 voters.

articles.title: How scared should we be now about cooperating with German intel?
articles.summary: German spy scandals are nothing new.
articles.body:
The arrest of August Hanning, the eighty-year-old former head of the German Federal Intelligence Service has sent shock waves throughout Germany, and no doubt among all intelligence agencies that worked with the service during his tenure.

German prosecutors accuse Hanning of espionage and treason — specifically, that he passed “highly sensitive situation assessments, classified material from foreign partner agencies and reportedly … papers on the Iranian nuclear program and the Russian military.”

So far, authorities have not revealed to whom he passed that material.

Also arrested is an official thus far named named only as “Manfred D,” who was Hanning’s chief of staff. When Hanning departed the service, Manfred D. remained at the agency for sixteen years before leaving it earlier this year. German prosecutors allege that during most of those years, he passed to Hanning some 2,000 documents containing sensitive and classified material and was remunerated for his efforts.

German spy scandals are nothing new. During the Cold War, the East German Stasi as well as the Soviet KGB penetrated the West German government, even at its highest levels. West German chancellor Willy Brandt, a hero of the anti-Nazi resistance, was forced to resign after his close aide, Gunter Guillaume, was arrested in April 1974 for acting as Stasi agent.

Again in 1990, Klaus Kuron, a senior German counterintelligence official, was convicted as a Stasi spy . Not surprisingly, the German-American intelligence relationship, never a truly comfortable one, has constantly been fraught with mutual suspicion.

Especially disturbing was the case of the supposed German intelligence asset nicknamed “Curveball” during the run-up to the Operation Iraqi Freedom. In 2002, Hanning passed on what he claimed was his source’s “reliable and convincing” evidence that the Iraqis possessed chemical and biological weapons. Ultimately the information was proven false.

Twenty-one years later, in 2023, a senior intelligence officer identified only as “Carsten L,” was accused of passing state secrets to Russia. Prosecutors claimed he had been paid to share intelligence about the Ukraine War and the now-defunct Wagner Group.

It is noteworthy that August Hanning’s leadership of the Federal Intelligence Service overlapped almost exactly with the 1998-2005 tenure of German Chancellor Gerhard Schroeder. Schroeder vocally opposed the Iraq war and refused to provide either financial or personnel support for the American effort. At the same time he had a warm relationship with Vladimir Putin; in 2004, he called him a “flawless democrat.”

After leaving the German government, Schroeder maintained close ties to Russia. He served on the board of the Nord Stream pipeline project, in which the Russian energy firm Gazprom owned a majority stake. He also served on the board of Rosneft, Russia’s leading petroleum producer and refiner.

Earlier this year, Putin proposed that Schroeder represent the European Union in possible talks with Russia. Perhaps not surprisingly, in light of Schroeder’s ongoing personal relationship with Putin, the EU rejected the idea.

Last week, at a time when Putin was ramping up his attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure and the West was contemplating further action against Moscow, Schroeder joined the supervisory board of the Russian supermarket chain Hyperglobus. Reflecting his very different view of Russian aggression, Schroeder reportedly stated that “it is exactly in these crisis times that these ties are especially important: they allow us to hear each other and look for ways forward.”

That Schroeder’s chancellorship and Hanning’s leadership of the intelligence service were coterminous is no indication that Schroeder was in any way connected with Hanning’s alleged betrayal. Moreover, it remains unclear to which country Hanning leaked sensitive material. Speculation has initially centered on Azerbaijan, not Russia. For its part, Baku has formally denied the allegation.

On the other hand, it is possible that Hanning believed that he could exploit the atmosphere that existed in the Schroeder chancellery without Schroeder’s knowledge.

Hanning’s arrest is certain to reinforce American qualms, and those of allied intelligence agencies, about cooperation with German intelligence. For example, Britain’s intelligence services are reportedly reviewing all sensitive information that they shared with allies during the period that Hanning and his chief of staff were active.

Nevertheless, despite legitimate concerns about what information Hanning illicitly passed to one or more as yet unidentified states, Western agencies should not freeze Germany out of all intelligence cooperation. The real beneficiary of such a move would be Putin’s Russia and other states hostile to the West.

Instead, intelligence agencies should adopt a cautious posture when interacting with German intelligence. Rather than press for a complete break, they would be wise to adopt President Ronald Reagan’s trademark maxim when he was dealing with the Soviet Union: “Trust, but verify.”

Dov S. Zakheim is a senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies and vice chairman of the board for the Foreign Policy Research Institute. He was undersecretary of Defense (comptroller) and chief financial officer for the Department of Defense from 2001 to 2004 and a deputy undersecretary of Defense from 1985 to 1987 .

articles.title: Trump approval sinks to 30 percent in new survey
articles.summary: President Trump’s approval rating dropped to 30 percent in a new Pew Research survey, amid growing dissatisfaction with his handling of foreign policy, the economy and immigration enforcement. Sixty-eight percent of respondents disapproved of the way Trump is handling his job, according to the survey, which was released Thursday. Trump’s approval rating has continually dropped…
articles.body:
President Trump’s approval rating dropped to 30 percent in a new Pew Research survey , amid growing dissatisfaction with his handling of foreign policy , the economy and immigration enforcement .

Sixty-eight percent of respondents disapproved of the way Trump is handling his job, according to the survey, which was released Thursday.

Trump’s approval rating has continually dropped since his return to the White House in 2025. Trump’s current rating is close to his lowest rating during his term, at 29 percent, following the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol attack in the final days of his term.

Pew Research noted that Trump’s approval rating was down among his 2024 supporters, particularly among younger and Hispanic voters. Fifty-seven percent of Trump’s 2024 Hispanic backers approve of his performance in office, while 69 percent of his 2024 voters overall approve of his handling of his job.

His approval rating among 2024 Trump voters aged 19 to 34 was 49 percent, compared with 76 percent of his 2024 voters aged 50 and older.

The survey found 69 percent of American respondents had little confidence the president could “keep his business interests separate from his presidential decision-making,” while 30 percent had confidence.

Confidence in the president’s handling of several key issues — including the economy, foreign policy and immigration — was lower than at the beginning of his term. For example, 35 percent of Americans surveyed now said they are very or somewhat confident in Trump to make good decisions about foreign policy — down 9 points since April 2025.

For his decisions regarding economic policy, 35 percent of U.S. respondents said they are very or somewhat confident in Trump to make good decisions, while 41 percent said Trump made good decisions about immigration.

The survey was conducted from Sept. 28 to Oct. 4 between 5,062 respondents. The margin of error was 1.6 percentage points.

Trump and Republicans are facing down the widely unpopular Iran war , a conflict that has stretched for more than seven months. The war has contributed to elevated prices, affecting inflation and causing gas prices to soar.

Trump said Thursday the U.S. military would not launch strikes against Iran before the midterm elections, adding the administration is having “productive discussions” with the Islamic Republic.

GOP candidates and lawmakers are also slowly distancing themselves from Trump amid growing frustration with tariffs against Canada causing the cost of goods to increase.

articles.title: Trump knocks Alaska voting system: ‘How stupid are we to do this?’
articles.summary: President Trump took to Truth Social on Thursday to encourage Alaskans to vote for the Republican ticket in November and criticized the state’s voting system in the process. Trump questioned why three Republicans are facing off against one Democrat in the November gubernatorial election, calling the system “stupid.” Alaskans approved a ballot measure in 2020…
articles.body:
President Trump took to Truth Social on Thursday to encourage Alaskans to vote for the Republican ticket in November and criticized the state’s voting system in the process.

Trump questioned why three Republicans are facing off against one Democrat in the November gubernatorial election, calling the system “stupid.” Alaskans approved a ballot measure in 2020 to create a nonpartisan primary election system where the top four vote-getters advance to a general election tallied with ranked-choice voting.

In November, Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins will face off against Republicans David Bronson, Treg Taylor, and Bernadette Wilson to be the next governor of Alaska. In the Senate race, former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska) will face off against incumbent Sen. Dan S. Sullivan (R-Alaska), Republican Gerald Heikes and Dan J. Sullivan, who holds no party affiliation.

Trump will travel to Alaska next week for a rally in Wasilla aimed at boosting support for Republicans. Alaskans will have the opportunity to repeal the top-four, ranked choice voting system via a ballot measure in November, which Trump supports.

A previous effort to repeal the system narrowly failed in 2024 .

“We have the Corrupt Ranked Choice System of Voting, which shouldn’t be allowed in our Country and will, hopefully, be repealed in the November Vote,” Trump said in his post.

There is no evidence that ranked choice voting is corrupt. Two states — Maine and Alaska — use the system statewide while New York City and Washington, D.C., use it for their primary elections.

Trump also voiced his support for the incumbent Sullivan and Republican Nick Begich, who is running for the at-large House seat. The Senate race has become competitive in the historically red state as Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) forecasts the race “leans in favor” of Peltola. DDHQ said Begich is likely to win the House seat.

“Alaska needs Senator Dan S. Sullivan in the Senate, and Congressman Nick Begich, in Congress — That is a fantastic team,” Trump said.

articles.body:
The Cook Political Report, an election handicapper, shifted 18 House seats toward Democrats’ favor in key battleground districts.

The changes show how unfavorable the political environment continues to be for GOP candidates amid the war in Iran and the state of the economy.

Republican Reps. Mariannette Miller-Meeks (Iowa), Zach Nunn (Iowa), Ryan Mackenzie (Pa.), Scott Perry (Pa.), Bill Huizenga (Mich.), Rob Wittman (Va.), Brian Fitzpatrick (Pa.), French Hill (Ark.) and Victoria Spartz (Ind.) all saw their races shifted toward Democrats.

At the same time, Democratic Reps. Susie Lee (Nev.), Tom Suozzi (N.Y.), Laura Gillen (N.Y.), Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (Wash.), Don Davis (N.C.) saw their races shift further in their party’s favor.

There are four open races in Nebraska’s 2nd District, Iowa’s 2nd District, Kentucky’s 6th District and Maine’s 2nd District that also shifted toward Democrats.

“With these new moves, we’re also adjusting our range: the most likely outcome is now that Democrats will pick up nine to 19 seats,” Cook Political Report’s U.S. House of Representatives editor Erin Covey wrote in an analysis. “At this point, Democrats only need to win 20 percent of the Toss Ups to get to a majority, assuming the seats that favor Democrats in our ratings all break their way.”

Based on Cook’s prediction, Democrats would hold anywhere from 224 to 234 seats.

Many congressional districts Cook Political Report shifted were ones that President Trump carried in each of his presidential bids, but growing dissatisfaction with his handling of the economy and foreign policy has created openings for Democrats in red-leaning districts.

“On paper, this open seat should be difficult for a Democrat to win,” Covey wrote about Kentucky’s 6th Congressional District. “Trump carried the district by 15 points, and [Rep. Andy Barr], now running for Senate, won reelection by 27 points. But polling from both parties shows Democratic prosecutor Zach Dembo and former Republican state Sen. Ralph Alvarado neck-and-neck.”

Trump’s economic approval rating has also dropped to historic lows amid the unpopular war against Iran, which is partly responsible for regular gas prices increasing to an average of $4.37 a gallon Friday, more than a 40 percent increase from a year ago, according to AAA .

The price of diesel, which is a primary fuel source for public transportation and the trucking industry, was up to around an average of $6.28 per gallon Friday. High prices of diesel impact rural parts of the country more.

Tariffs against U.S. trading partners, particularly Canada, have also hit states like Michigan , Wisconsin and Maine hard as U.S. trade with Canada totaled an estimated $872.3 billion in 2025, according to the U.S. Trade Representative’s Office .

articles.title: Pretend Orban is on the ballot — he offered handouts, too
articles.summary: Whether it’s Trump, Orbán or Vance, opening the fiscal purse to appease a grumbling public is a classic move made by history’s practitioners of clientelism.
articles.body:
“Pretend, please, I’m on the ballot,” said President Trump.

It has become a common refrain at rallies, and it is how he kicked off the Republican midterm convention. The strategy is, since Trump always does well in elections, voters just need to fool themselves into thinking he’s on the ballot and the Republicans will not lose their majority in Congress.

Meanwhile the White House’s new television ad , proudly stamped with “paid for by the U.S. Government,” shows Trump moving intensely before the camera as a voice-over pitches viewers to join his “final battle” to “demolish the deep state” and “expel the warmongers from our government.”

Taking millions of taxpayer dollars that Congress had already appropriated for other uses to instead pay for a partisan campaign ad?

“I hate it,” Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) said , “I tell you, it feels like Vicktor Orban talking to the Hungarian people.”

The reference to Orbán may be an apt one. After 16 years in power, late in 2025, Orban began to realize that his April reelection bid was in jeopardy. Orban started to hand out political giveaways . He put a cap on mortgage interest rates , subsidized housing of public-sector workers, exempted young voters and mothers from income tax, topped off pensions and injected cash into restaurants and tourism.

His party lost in a landslide . Orban has been out of power since.

Trump has a similar tendency when he gets squeezed politically — to try to buy his way to victory with taxpayer-funded giveaways. This explains his infamous pledge to pay each adult a $5,000 dividend if Republicans hold onto both chambers. It also curiously brings to mind Vice President JD Vance’s proposal to make transfer payments to stay-at-home spouses — but not to single working parents.

Both schemes are set up as cash transfers, making Orbán’s earnings-contingent payout look politically tame by comparison. Trump and Vance are really swinging for the fences.

Budget hawks have picked apart both giveaway proposals. Legal scholars have also weighed in about the gray area surrounding the television ads.

The Hatch Act of 1939 bars partisan political activity by federal employees, and Congress prohibits appropriated funds from supporting “ publicity or propaganda ”. One legal scholar said the content of the ads fails that basic test between legitimate public information versus partisan electioneering. Several watchdog groups have filed complaints , but it seems doubtful these will be resolved by election day.

Meanwhile, defenders of the ads say they are merely public service announcements, not propaganda at all, and they don’t violate campaign finance law because Trump is not a candidate on the November ballot.

In my field of study, public choice theory, these giveaway maneuvers are recognized as classic features of clientelism , typical of small country dictators and urban political bosses desperate to keep power.

Peronism in Argentina is one example, where make-work jobs were created in exchange for votes. Some provinces in India also exemplify clientelism, where it is not uncommon for incumbents to distribute cash and goods prior to elections. In the U.S. industrial era, job-patronage regimes including Tammany Hall in New York and the Daley machine in Chicago both exemplify the essence of clientelism.

Whether it’s Trump, Orban or Vance, opening the fiscal purse to appease a grumbling public is a classic move made by history’s practitioners of clientelism.

Who is on the ballot this midterm election? It might not make a difference whether we pretend it’s Orbán or Trump. But it will make a big difference if we reject clientelism and move on with our lives in America’s constitutional republic.

I am not one to predict election outcomes. But, like anyone else, I do see polls and expert commentary leaning against the Republicans keeping their majority. This will create a policy window of opportunity. America is weary of Trump’s glare, and voters are hungry for something that makes sense. Who knows whether the Democrats will deliver.

Edward Lopez is a senior fellow and director of entrepreneurship and innovation at Independent Institute in Oakland, Calif., and professor of Economics at Western Carolina University.

articles.title: Trump establishes ‘committee of inquiry’ for Federal Reserve member Lisa Cook
articles.summary: President Trump established a committee Friday to investigate whether Federal Reserve board of governors member Lisa Cook “made false statements in connection with one or more mortgage instruments.” The “committee of inquiry” will hold an in-person hearing next month to consider the allegations and evidence against her. The committee is made up of the assistant…
articles.body:
President Trump established a committee Friday to investigate whether Federal Reserve board of governors member Lisa Cook “made false statements in connection with one or more mortgage instruments.”

The “committee of inquiry” will hold an in-person hearing next month to consider the allegations and evidence against her. The committee is made up of the assistant to the president for economic policy, the chair of the equal employment opportunity commission and the director of the office of government ethics.

“As President, it is my job to ensure the laws are faithfully executed, including by firing subordinates who cannot be trusted to tell the truth and follow the law,” Trump wrote in a memo .

It said Cook should appear at the hearing and can “present argument, written evidence, and written witness statements regarding the evidence and allegations.”

“In light of the President’s repeated statements that he has already decided to fire Governor Cook — regardless of the facts and evidence — we have grave doubts that this “hearing” is a legitimate one that would conform to the law,” Cook’s attorneys Abbe Lowell and Norm Eisen said in a statement.

“But if it is anything close to objective, the conclusion will be that Governor Cook did not commit mortgage fraud, leaving no cause to remove her from the Federal Reserve Board,” the duo wrote.

They added that they’ve engaged with the White House to determine if this process is a “genuine one and not simply a box checking exercise.”

“Governor Cook welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name and demonstrate there is no legal basis to fire her,” the attorneys noted.

The administration attempted to fire her in August 2025 after Federal Housing Finance Agency Director Bill Pulte issued a referral suggesting she illegally designated her properties in Georgia and Michigan as her primary residences to get lower mortgage rates.

The Supreme Court ruled 5-4 in June that she could stay in her position because she did not receive enough due process to contest the allegations.

She denies the claims against her and said she erroneously referred to one of two properties as a “vacation home.” Cook has said the firing was spurred by the president’s frustrations over the Fed not lowering interest rates quickly enough.

This announcement marks the latest escalation in the administration’s efforts to oust her from the central bank. After the high court’s ruling, Trump vowed to “take appropriate action immediately.”

“The Cook Lawsuit, having to do with her suitability in sitting on the Board of the Federal Reserve, was sent back by the Supreme Court on a strictly procedural basis, we will take appropriate action immediately to make sure that someone who has committed wrongdoing will not be making vital decisions concerning the Welfare of the United States of America!” Trump wrote on Truth Social at the time.

It’s Friday. The leaves will soon be falling, but right now, the weekend is calling. 🍂

This year’s Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to Navi Pillay , a leading figure in international human rights law, coming as Israel and the U.S. seek to tear down the institutions she has helped build up.

“At a time of existential challenges – including more wars and conflicts than the world has seen in a long time – international law is no longer just a supplement to peace and security. It is an absolute necessity,” the committee wrote in its announcement.

“And yet, the system of international law is under tremendous pressure, and its institutions are under attack. We see a shift towards power politics at the expense of legal frameworks and global respect for law and justice.”

Pillay’s resume: The jurist previously served as the United Nations human rights chief and was a judge at the International Criminal Court (ICC).

As a judge at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, she helped establish that sexual violence and propaganda could constitute genocide.

She is currently an ad hoc judge at the International Court of Justice, in a case alleging that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya ethnic minority.

Perhaps most controversially, Pillay led a U.N. commission that found last year that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza.

Angry reactions: Israel’s government fumed over the choice.

“If there were an award for lies, hatred, and blood libels, Navi Pillay wouldn’t just be a contender. She’d be a frontrunner. Her role in the relentless, politically motivated demonization of Israel and promotion of the genoLIE speaks volumes,” Israel’s Foreign Ministry wrote in a post on the social platform X .

President Trump shared a post from attorney David Schoen , who worked on his second impeachment trial.

“Today the Nobel Committee shamed itself beyond repair and demeaned the once great Nobel Peace Prize by giving it to the UN’s Navi Pillay. Pillay is an unabashed hater of America and Israel,” Schoen wrote in a post on Truth Social .

Timely move: Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced Friday that the U.S. is imposing full blocking sanctions against the ICC, escalating its fight against the global judicial body.

“We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling their ability to operate against us,” Rubio said in a video message.

Pillay had Trump on her mind shortly after learning she won the prize.

“If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump,” Pillay said in a video clip shared from the moment she heard the news in Nuremberg, Germany.

Last year’s prize winner, Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado , presented her award to Trump in Washington after the president openly coveted the honor.

Trump’s team did not make a public push for the prize this year.

Forget polite exchanges about policy. Thursday night’s Senate debates in Georgia , Michigan and Maine turned into a string of personal attacks, heated accusations and some memorable clashes.

In the Peach State, Sen. Jon Ossoff (D) repeatedly called his Republican challenger Rep. Mike Collins a “bigot” — accusing him of promoting extremist content online. Collins condemned racism and antisemitism but hit back by calling Ossoff a “trust fund kid” who can’t relate to Georgians struggling with high prices.

In Michigan, former GOP Rep. Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed couldn’t even stop arguing during a commercial break.

“In 30 years of doing debates, I’ve never seen it continue during the commercial,” said moderator Rick Albin , from Nexstar’s WOOD TV in Grand Rapids, Mich.

El-Sayed labeled Rogers a “sock puppet” of Trump , while the Republican questioned his progressive opponent’s medical credentials and made an unsubstantiated allegation about ties to the Muslim Brotherhood.

Maine had its own blowup : Sen. Susan Collins (R) demanded an apology after Democrat Troy Jackson accused her and her husband of making money off the Iran war — a claim he didn’t substantiate.

“No, you owe me an apology,” Jackson shot back.

The common threads? Trump, the Middle East conflict and voters’ frustration over rising costs.

Trump is ramping up his midterm campaign appearances just as new polls reveal growing cracks in his support — including among voters who helped elect him.

A new Politico-PF Global poll found 26 percent of the president’s 2024 voters think GOP candidates would have a better shot in November if they broke with him on certain issues, such as the economy, immigration enforcement and the Iran war.

And there’s more : The latest Reuters/Ipsos poll found 78 percent of Americans, including 64 percent of Republicans, hold the administration at least partly responsible for rising costs. Nearly 6 in 10 GOP respondents in particular said their living expenses are rising faster than their paychecks, according to the data.

Meanwhile, Trump is headed to Syracuse, N.Y., Friday to campaign alongside Republican gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman , following recent stops in Alabama, Nebraska and Texas. This week he added upcoming stops in Ohio, Alaska and Arizona.

The timing is particularly tricky for Republicans, who are now defending Senate seats in states like Kansas and Iowa that weren’t expected to be competitive just months ago.

U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle is under scrutiny over allegations she sought $100,000 from a Trump donor to pay off credit card debt in exchange for political access. Her attorney disputes the authenticity of messages at the center of the allegations.

🔎Read more about the MAGA donor, Eric Deters , here.

The controversy overshadowed Rubio’s visit to Greece, while Democrats and at least one Senate Republican are demanding an investigation into her conduct.

It adds to a growing list of questions about the business dealings of the president’s allies, including two White House advisers who reportedly worked for a pro-Russia political party in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Trump has threatened to fire them if conflicts of interest are found.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth ‘s decision to livestream the upcoming execution of convicted Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan is drawing sharp backlash from lawmakers on both sides of the aisle.

Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) isn’t questioning whether Hasan deserves the death penalty — but why the Pentagon wants to turn it into a public spectacle.

“Beyond disgusting,” Tillis wrote late Thursday, comparing the move to public executions carried out by oppressive dictatorships.

And he’s not alone. Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.) called the idea “medieval,” asking whether the Pentagon chief was trying to mimic ISIS executions.

The backdrop: Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist convicted of killing 13 people at the Fort Hood base in Texas in 2009, is scheduled to face a firing squad on Dec. 3 after Trump approved the action earlier this week. Hegseth argues that making it public will show people there are “serious consequences” for such crimes.

Historical wrinkle: The U.S. hasn’t held a public execution since 1936.

articles.title: To strengthen child welfare and keep families together, we need structural change
articles.summary: A new framework from United Family Advocates argues that federal child welfare financing requires significant reform to prioritize community-based support over the costly and harmful practice of separating families.
articles.body:
For decades, policymakers have built federal child welfare policy brick by brick, relying on outdated assumptions about what the government should do when children and families struggle. They have designed programs and prescribed resources, while rigid funding structures have bound these layers together.

Over time, this structure has hardened in place, despite overwhelming data that challenges the child welfare financing institution and its corresponding incentives. Today, more than 2 million American families are investigated by Child Protective Services each year.

In 84 percent of those cases , there is no substantiated finding of abuse or neglect. Yet every year, approximately 175,000 children enter foster care , despite decades of outcomes that show the harm the intervention itself causes, and even when we now know there is no association between foster care entries and child maltreatment fatalities.

For Nate Bustamente, family separation was an inescapable throughline in his life. Bustamente entered foster care as a child, and years later, after becoming a parent himself, he and his wife faced a child welfare case involving their own children. He worked long hours to meet the requirements imposed on his family while navigating the possibility of losing his children. After a second removal, the state pursued termination of his and his wife’s parental rights. Despite months of compliance, they still had to defend their right to remain a family in court.

Bustamente credits his attorney and the family-time supervisor who observed his family’s visits with helping the court understand what was happening in their lives. The judge denied the termination petition, and the case eventually closed. Reflecting on that moment, Bustamente described how he could finally breathe without carrying the weight of what might happen to his family — an experience facing too many families caught in the crosshairs of an unforgiving system.

United Family Advocates, a bipartisan group of child welfare advocates, attorneys, researchers and nonprofit leaders, recently released a framework to shed light on how federal child welfare financing is structured in ways that too often make family separations like Bustamente’s the path of least resistance, when it should be the last resort.

As federal policymakers increasingly examine whether existing child welfare funding mechanisms adequately support child safety, family stability, and responsible stewardship of taxpayer dollars, it is clear that the patchwork that created the fundamental financing structure we have today needs significant reform. The current structure is an entitlement program, and functions as a $10 billion entitlement to separate families.

States need greater flexibility to invest in the community-based supports families actually need to address housing, food, mental health, substance use, or other challenges, while preserving a clear role for protecting children facing imminent danger. Funding should also include resources families can access without having to enter the child welfare system, and access to high-quality legal representation to help ensure families have fair processes when such highly consequential decisions about their children and family are being made.

Federal policymakers have important debates ahead of them about what proportion of federal resources should go toward maintaining a system that responds to family crises versus building the infrastructure that helps families avoid those crises in the first place.

For Bustamente, a continuum of community support to address his family’s needs without making separation the default response could have changed the trajectory of his life. His question is simple: How many more families have to go through what he went through? The constant fear and the lost time with his children are not inevitable.

For decades, policymakers have added brick after brick to sustain a system that relies on separation as its primary intervention. It is time to stop reinforcing the status quo and start rebuilding a foundation that gives families the support they need before crisis becomes separation.
